d: Athenian, belonging to Athens.
me: Adjective, Nominative, Plural, Masculine
Adjective, Vocative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: “Athenian” refers to a person from Athens. It identifies people associated with that city, especially its inhabitants or citizens. In the Greek New Testament, the word appears twice, both times in Acts 17, describing people in Athens. The word itself names their connection to the city rather than expressing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a person from Athens.

d: To postpone, defer, especially: to postpone the trial of.
me: Verb, second Aorist, Middle, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: The word means “to adjourn a proceeding” or “to defer,” describing the decision to postpone a formal hearing or matter rather than continue it immediately. It functions as an action word: someone delays the proceeding until a later time. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 24:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is postponement of an official proceeding.

d: (a) to carry up, lead up, (b) to offer up (on a high altar) as a sacrifice, offer up to God on high.

e.t: This word means “to carry up” or “to lead up,” describing movement from a lower place or position to a higher one. It can refer to someone being brought upward, led upward, or something being carried upward. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times in 9 verses. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on what or whom it describes and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains upward movement or bringing something upward.

e.h: To Endure or Put Up With
e.t: This word means “to endure” or “to put up with” someone or something. It describes continuing to bear a situation, person, or difficulty rather than refusing it immediately. As a verb, it expresses the action of patiently tolerating or enduring. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 14 times, so its exact force depends on what or whom a person is called to bear in each passage.

d: Repudiation, divorce; bill of divorce.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Neuter
Noun, Genitive, Singular, Neuter

e.t: The word means “divorce,” referring to the ending of a marriage. It names this marital action directly, rather than describing a general disagreement or ordinary distance between people. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, appearing twice in Matthew and once in Mark. Its references are Matthew 5:31, Matthew 19:7, and Mark 10:4. These references locate the word, while the surrounding verse determines how the subject is being discussed.

e.t: This word means “be full,” describing something that contains or is filled with something. It can also be rendered “is full” or “to be full,” so its basic idea is a state of fullness rather than an action of filling. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times and is used across Matthew, Luke, Romans, and Revelation. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is described as full.

d: (Physical) exercise, in a wide sense.
me: Noun, Nominative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “training,” referring to the practice of developing strength or ability through disciplined exercise. It presents training as an activity or process rather than as a person or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Timothy 4:8. Its precise emphasis in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the deliberate practice of training, especially in contrast with something left undeveloped or neglected.

d: To be in trouble, doubt, difficulty; to be at a loss.
me: Verb, Imperfect, Active, Indicative, third, Plural
Verb, Imperfect, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means to be perplexed—to be confused, uncertain, or unable to understand what is happening. It describes a person facing something puzzling and not knowing how to make sense of it or what to do. In the Greek New Testament, it appears four times, each time describing perplexity rather than a settled conclusion or clear understanding. The word can describe the reaction of individuals or groups when events, reports, or circumstances seem difficult to explain. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: To be peaceful, keep the peace, to be at peace.
me: Verb, Present, Active, iMperative, second, Plural
Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “be at peace” or “to live in peace.” It describes a peaceful condition and can express the call to maintain peace in one’s conduct toward others. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in Mark, Romans, 2 Corinthians, and 1 Thessalonians. Its wording presents peace as something people are to live in or pursue, while the surrounding verse determines the specific situation being addressed.

d: A waiting for, expectation.
me: Noun, Nominative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “expectation”: an anticipated outcome or something looked toward with anticipation. It functions as a noun, naming what is awaited rather than describing an action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so this single occurrence represents its known use in that corpus. It appears in Hebrews 10:27, but the word’s precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage rather than on the word alone.

e.t: This word means to hope or expect something with confidence. It describes looking ahead toward what is desired or anticipated, rather than merely thinking about the future. In the New Testament, it is used 31 times, showing a recurring expression for hopeful expectation. The word can describe people hoping for what God has promised, waiting for a future outcome, or expecting a visit or result. Its exact emphasis in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to fill up” or “to provide.” It describes something being made full, supplied, or brought to completeness. In its five New Testament occurrences, it can refer to people being filled, a supply being provided, or something reaching the needed amount. The word appears in Luke, John, Acts, and Romans, so its basic sense is used across several kinds of passages. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being filled or provided there.

d: To revel (in), live luxuriously, riot.
me: Verb, Present, middle or passive depoNent, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This verb means “to revel”: to take lively, uninhibited pleasure in something, often with open enjoyment. It describes an active response rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 2:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on exuberant enjoyment or celebration.

d: (a) to dig out, hence: to open up, (b) to gouge.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to dig out” or “to dig through.” It describes removing earth or breaking through a barrier by digging. The idea is active and practical: someone makes an opening or clears a way by excavation. It occurs two times in the Greek New Testament, in Mark 2:4 and Galatians 4:15. In ordinary reading, its precise force depends on whether the sentence emphasizes creating an opening, removing material, or bringing something out through digging.

d: Eager longing (desire), strong affection.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “longing”: a strong inward desire for someone or something. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in 2 Corinthians 7, and English rendering supports the same meaning in each occurrence. The word therefore describes an earnest desire rather than a casual preference. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a heartfelt longing directed toward a person or desired outcome.

It is an action word describing the act of setting, placing, or laying something down or upon another thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 39 times, so its precise emphasis depends on what is being placed and the surrounding sentence. Its range includes ordinary acts of putting or laying, without requiring a special figurative meaning.

d: To rest from work, cease from altercation, to be silent, live quietly.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means to be quiet, become silent, or give up pressing an action. It can describe stopping speech, ceasing activity, or yielding so that something else may proceed, depending on the sentence. The word appears five times in the Greek New Testament, in Luke, Acts, and 1 Thessalonians. Its basic idea is restraint: becoming still rather than continuing to speak, act, or resist. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

d: (Hebrew), Jacob, (a) the patriarch, son of Isaac, (b) father of Joseph, the husband of Mary.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Masculine, Person
Noun, Genitive, Singular, Masculine, Person
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Masculine, Person

e.t: Jacob is a personal name referring to Jacob, the patriarch known throughout the Bible. In the Greek New Testament, it remains a name rather than a description or action. It appears 27 times in the New Testament, including genealogies and passages that speak of Jacob alongside Isaac and Abraham. The name occurs from Matthew through Hebrews, showing its use when the New Testament recalls Jacob and the people connected with him.

d: To overpower, quell, treat harshly.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Plural
Verb, Present, Passive, Participle, Accusative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word describes oppressing people—using power to burden, mistreat, or take advantage of them. It can also be rendered “to exploit,” emphasizing unfair treatment for someone else’s benefit. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, once in Acts and once in James, showing a consistent sense of people being subjected to oppressive treatment. The word focuses on harmful action against others rather than merely describing difficulty or hardship.

d: Garb, clothing, dress, attire.
me: Noun, Dative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word refers to a person’s appearance, clothing, or outward conduct. Its meanings include “appearance,” “attire,” and “attire/behaviour,” so it can point beyond garments to the way someone presents himself or herself. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Timothy 2:9. Its precise emphasis in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the word functions there.

d: To be in danger or peril.
me: Verb, Imperfect, Active, Indicative, third, Plural
Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, first, Plural
Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “be in danger” or “to be in danger.” It describes being exposed to a serious threat or facing circumstances that could bring harm. The word appears four times in the Greek New Testament, in Luke, Acts, and 1 Corinthians. Its use can describe danger affecting people, situations, or what someone values, but the exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage. It is a verb expressing the condition of facing danger, rather than simply naming danger as an abstract idea.

d: To abate, cease raging, to be stilled.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to abate” or “to die down”—to become less intense until the force or disturbance has subsided. It describes a change from active strength or turmoil toward quietness, rather than simply stopping by command. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew and Mark, and each occurrence belongs to an account involving changing conditions. Its precise force in any one verse is understood from the surrounding passage.

d: Secretly, privately.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means doing something quietly or secretly, without making it openly known. It describes the manner in which an action, conversation, or inquiry takes place rather than naming the action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, and each occurrence is rendered “secretly.” The word can therefore point to conduct carried out away from public notice, whether to avoid attention, to speak privately, or to act without openly revealing the matter. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This word refers to a sage or sorcerer—a person presented as possessing special knowledge or practicing magic. Its exact sense is determined by the surrounding passage: it can identify the visitors who came to Jesus as a child or a man opposed to the gospel. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, in Matthew and Acts, and is commonly rendered “sorcerer.”

me: Noun, Accusative, Plural, Feminine
Noun, Nominative, Plural, Feminine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “quarrel”: a dispute or contention between people. It describes strife as something that can exist among individuals or arise from competing desires, while its surrounding context determines the particular situation. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in 2 Corinthians, 2 Timothy, Titus, and James. Its central sense remains a quarrel or conflict rather than peaceful disagreement.

d: To change my position, depart, remove.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to leave” or “to move on.” It describes departing from one place and going elsewhere, so its basic sense is movement away rather than remaining. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Matthew. The surrounding passage determines who is leaving and where the movement leads, but the word itself expresses a change of place or departure. It is a straightforward action word describing someone moving on from a location.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “wage.” It refers to payment or reward given in response to something done, whether viewed as compensation or as what is received from an action. The word occurs 29 times in the Greek New Testament, across 28 verses, from Matthew through Revelation. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains what a person receives as a wage or reward.

It is used as an adjective, so it identifies the condition or character of a person, thing, or situation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 24 times across 21 verses, showing a recurring contrast between what is new and what is old. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains newness or freshness.

d: A night and day, twenty-four hours.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: “A night and a day” refers to a complete period that includes both nighttime and daytime. It functions as a time expression rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. The expression appears in 2 Corinthians 11:25, but understanding its specific force there requires the surrounding verse and passage.

Its exact sense depends on what it describes: it can refer broadly to people or things, or to every member considered individually. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 1,243 times, showing that this is a common word for expressing totality or completeness. It appears from Matthew through Revelation.

e.t: This word means “five hundred,” expressing the specific number 500. It is a numerical term rather than a description of a person, action, or spiritual quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, showing the same basic numerical meaning in both places. Its exact significance in any sentence comes from the quantity being counted in that surrounding passage. The word appears in Luke 7:41 and 1 Corinthians 15:6. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and its use there.

In the Greek New Testament, it appears five times, referring to deceptive people or influences. Its sense points to deliberate error or misleading conduct, so the surrounding passage identifies what is being denied, distorted, or falsely presented. The word is used in passages ranging from Matthew to 2 John, showing that warning against deception is a recurring New Testament concern.

e.t: This word means “to beat with a rod.” It describes physical punishment carried out with a stick or staff, focusing on the act of striking rather than naming the instrument itself. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 16:22 and 2 Corinthians 11:25. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the experience or action of being beaten with a rod.

d: A moth.
me: Noun, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “moth,” the name of a small insect. It is a concrete noun referring to the creature itself rather than to an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times: twice in Matthew and once in Luke. Its exact force in each sentence comes from the surrounding verse, but its basic lexical meaning remains “moth.”

The central idea is an identifiable item or person considered in terms of its use, ownership, or role. Its precise significance in any particular sentence comes from the surrounding verse and passage.

The central idea is purposeful joining rather than remaining separate, whether the word concerns parts brought together or people sharing in unity. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: once in 1 Corinthians 12:24 and once in Hebrews 4:2. The surrounding verse identifies exactly what is being joined, but the word itself points clearly to combination and unity.

d: To compel, urge, force together.
me: Verb, Imperfect, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to reconcile” or “to urge.” It describes an action that seeks to bring people toward agreement, peace, or restored relationship, and it can also express urging someone toward a response. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 7:26. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is either restoring agreement or pressing people to accept it.

Its exact object and force in a particular passage depend on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains honor and respectful valuing.

d: To surpass, excel, exceed, transcend.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “surpasses,” “surpassing,” or “to go beyond.” It describes something that rises above a comparison or exceeds an expected measure. In its five New Testament occurrences, it is used in passages speaking of what is greater than something else, including the surpassing greatness of power and love. The word therefore points to excellence, abundance, or greatness that goes beyond an ordinary limit. Its exact force in any verse is shaped by what is being compared.

d: (literal: light-bearing), radiant, the morning-star.

e.t: This word means “light-bearing,” describing something that carries, gives, or displays light. It is a descriptive word rather than a general term for light itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 1:19. Without the verse text and surrounding context, its precise force in that passage cannot be explained further here; however, its central idea remains clear: something associated with bringing light or shining. The word therefore points readers toward brightness, illumination, or the bearer of light, according to the sentence in which it appears.

d: Apart from, separately from; without.
me: PREPosition

e.t: This word means “without” or “by itself.” It marks the absence of someone or something, or describes something considered apart from another. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 41 times, so it serves as a recurring way to express separation, independence, or lack of accompaniment. Its exact force depends on what person or thing is being described as absent or separate in the sentence. The word appears across several New Testament books, including Matthew, John, Romans, Hebrews, and James.

me: Verb, Future, Middle, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to come in” or “to enter,” describing movement into a place or situation. It is an action word, focusing on arrival from outside rather than simply being present. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 21:35. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the act of coming into or entering something.
